# Build your own agent in R {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

*Self-study: about 45 minutes, not part of the timed day.*

All day you have worked with Claude Code. At its core it is a model, a
`r glossary("harness")` and a few `r glossary("tools")` in a loop.
On this page you build that loop yourself in R, in under 100 lines, with the
ellmer package. Once you have built it, every control from Blocks 4 to 6 is
something you can see in your own code: what Manual mode approves, what a deny
rule blocks, and what leaves your machine.

The page follows the order of Hadley Wickham's explainer
[*What is an agent?*](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/what-is-an-agent): first a
conversation, then a tool, then the loop. Joseph Barbier's talk *50 lines of
code to rebuild Claude Code in R* builds the same kind of agent; the version
here is our own.


## Before you start

You need:

- **ellmer**, which talks to Claude and runs the loop: `install.packages("ellmer")`.
  The agent also uses callr and fs, which the course install script includes.
- **An Anthropic API key** from a Console account. A Claude Pro or Max
  subscription does not include API use.
  ellmer reads it from the environment variable `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Open your
  user-level `.Renviron` with `usethis::edit_r_environ()`, add the line
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here`, save, and restart R.
- **The key kept out of every repository.** Your user-level `.Renviron` is
  outside your projects; never paste the key into a script. The workshop
  repository's `.gitignore` lists `.Renviron`, and its deny rule
  `Read(/.Renviron)` stops Claude Code reading a project copy
  ([Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)).

Every request costs money. `chat$get_cost()` shows what a conversation has
cost so far, so check it after each task. The code names its
model explicitly, `claude-opus-5-5`, so your AI-use log can record it; you can
swap in another Claude model ID.


## A conversation is turns

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-opus-5-5")
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat
```

Printing `chat` shows the conversation as a list of
`r glossary("turn", "turns")`, in pairs: your user turn, then the model's
assistant turn. `chat$get_turns()` returns them as R objects.

The second question works because of the harness, not the model. The model
keeps nothing between requests, so for each new question ellmer sends the
**whole conversation so far**. That is why a long conversation costs more per
question: you pay for every `r glossary("token")` of it again. It is also the
[context window](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd) from Block 1, seen from
the inside.


## A tool is an R function, run on your computer

A model can only produce text. A tool lets it ask for something to be done:

```{r}
#| eval: false
today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-opus-5-5")
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days until 25 December?")
```

The model never sees your function, only its name and description, so the
description is everything it knows about the tool. When it wants the date, its
reply is not an answer but a request: "call `today` with no arguments". ellmer
runs `today()` **on your computer** and sends the result back in a new user
turn. The model then answers, using the date it was given.

That is two `r glossary("round", "rounds")` for one question: one request that
ended in a tool request, and one that ended in the answer.
`chat$get_rounds()` shows them.


## The loop, with no model at all

You can run this section without an API key. It replaces the model with a
pretend one that follows a script, so that you can see the loop the harness
runs. Each pass of `repeat` is one round.

```{r}
# the tools, as plain R functions
tools <- list(
  n_rows = function(name) {
    nrow(get(name, envir = as.environment("package:datasets")))
  }
)

# a pretend model: asks for a tool until it has two results, then answers
pretend_model <- function(turns) {
  results <- Filter(function(t) t$role == "tool result", turns)
  if (length(results) == 0) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "mtcars"))
  } else if (length(results) == 1) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "iris"))
  } else {
    list(role = "assistant",
         text = paste("iris has", results[[2]]$text, "rows and mtcars has",
                      results[[1]]$text, "so iris has more."))
  }
}

# the harness: send the conversation, run any tool asked for, repeat
question <- "Which has more rows, mtcars or iris?"
turns <- list(list(role = "user", text = question))
repeat {
  reply <- pretend_model(turns)
  turns <- c(turns, list(reply))
  if (is.null(reply$tool)) break # no tool asked for: this is the answer
  result <- do.call(tools[[reply$tool]], reply$args)
  turns <- c(turns, list(list(role = "tool result", text = result)))
}

for (t in turns) {
  what <- if (is.null(t$tool)) t$text else
    paste0("call ", t$tool, "(", t$args, ")")
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", t$role, what))
}
```

Three things to notice:

- **The model only asks.** `do.call()` in the harness is the only line that
  does anything to your computer. Every control in the course acts at that
  line: Manual mode asks you before it runs, a deny rule refuses it, a hook
  inspects it.
- **Results go back to the model.** Whatever a tool returns joins the
  conversation, and the conversation is sent to the provider. That is
  [Block 4's disclosure route](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd): a tool
  that reads a data file sends that data.
- **The model decides when to stop.** The loop ends when a reply asks for no
  tool. A real model can also loop for longer than you expected, which is why
  a real harness has limits and a stop key.

In the real API the tool result goes back inside a user turn; ellmer does that
for you.


## What an agent is

An `r glossary("agent")` is a model in a harness, calling tools in a loop.
Read tools let it look around: list files, read them. Write tools let it change
things: edit a file, run code. With both, it can explore, make a change, check
the result and try again, which is what Claude Code did for you all day.

The write tools are where the risk is. Wickham's article warns with a tool
that deletes files: give an agent one without confirmation and it may use it.


## Build a mini coding agent

The agent below has four tools and three safeguards. Download it and save it
**outside your workshop repository**, for example in your Downloads folder, so
the agent cannot edit its own rules, just as Block 6 protects
`.claude/settings.json`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
downloadthis::download_file(
  path = here::here("files", "agent", "mini_agent.R"),
  output_name = "mini_agent",
  output_extension = ".R",
  button_label = "Download mini_agent.R",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)
```

The walkthrough below explains each part of the file.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reference: the full mini_agent.R

```{r, eval = FALSE, file = here::here("files", "agent", "mini_agent.R")}
```
:::

Each part matches something you met during the day:

- **Read and write tools.** `list_files()` and `read_file()` only observe;
  `tool_annotations(read_only_hint = TRUE)` labels them, but a label is only a
  hint and enforces nothing. `write_file()` and `run_r()` change things.
- **`inside_project()` is the agent's deny rule.** Every file tool calls it,
  and it refuses paths outside the project, under `data/raw/`, or to a
  credentials file (`.Renviron` or `.env`, in any folder). An error in a
  tool does not stop the agent: ellmer sends the error message back to the
  model, which can try something else.
- **`ask_first()` is Manual mode.** `chat$on_tool_request()` runs it before
  every tool call. Read calls go straight through; for a write or a run it
  prints the arguments, the file contents or the code, and calls
  `tool_reject()` unless you choose **Yes**.
- **`run_r()` uses a fresh R session.** `callr::r()` runs the code in a new
  R process, so it cannot change the objects in yours, and only the first 60
  lines of output go back to the model.
- **The system prompt is its `AGENTS.md`.** The
  `r glossary("system prompt")` is sent with every request, and like an
  instruction file it is only a request.

`run_r()` shows the limit Block 6 found in deny rules. `inside_project()`
guards the file tools, but R code run by `run_r()` can write anywhere, `data/raw/`
included. Only your approval stands in the way, which is why you read the code
before you choose **Yes**, and why the raw-data checksum test checks the result
whatever route a change took.


:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Run your agent (20 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** your workshop repository open in RStudio or Positron, committed and
clean in the Git pane. If `scripts/explore_voles.R` already has a
`mass_change_g` line from Block 4, delete that line and commit first. The
working directory must be the repository's root, as it is when you open the
project.

**1. Load the agent.** In the R console, with the path to where you saved it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
source("~/Downloads/mini_agent.R")
```

**2. Give it the task.**

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat$chat(paste(
  "Add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g) to the voles",
  "data in scripts/explore_voles.R, then run",
  "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R') to check it."
))
```

**3. Watch and decide.** The read calls run without asking. For each
`write_file` or `run_r` request, read what it prints, then choose **Yes** only
if you would have written it yourself. Try choosing **No** once and watch how
the agent responds.

**4. Look inside.** In the console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat                # the turns, with tokens and cost
chat$get_rounds()   # one entry per request to the model
chat$get_cost()
```

**5. Check its work.** Open the Git pane and read the diff of
`explore_voles.R`. Then run the test yourself in a fresh session, as in
[checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work):

```{r}
#| eval: false
callr::r(\(f) testthat::test_file(f), list(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R")))
```

**6. Record it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`, for example:

```
2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-opus-5-5); added mass_change_g; kept after reading the diff and running the test
```

**You are done when** the test passes when you run it yourself, the Git pane
shows only the change you approved, and you can say how many rounds the task
took and what it cost.

**If it goes wrong:** if the agent changed something you did not want, revert
the file in the Git pane. If `chat_anthropic()` reports a missing key, check
`Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") != ""` and restart R after editing
`.Renviron`. If the agent refuses a path you expected it to reach, check
`getwd()` is the repository's root.

::::
:::


## What Claude Code adds

| Your mini agent | Claude Code |
|---|---|
| `ask_first()` and `tool_reject()` | Manual mode (`default`) and the other permission modes |
| `inside_project()` | Deny rules in `.claude/settings.json`, such as `Read(/.Renviron)` |
| The system prompt | `AGENTS.md`, read at the start of each session |
| `run_r()` in a fresh R session with `callr::r()` | Commands it runs in the Terminal; you check results in a fresh R session |
| `get_turns()`, `get_rounds()`, `get_cost()` | The conversation itself, and the model shown above the prompt |
| Git | Git |

Claude Code also has what this agent lacks: plan mode, hooks, skills,
compaction of long conversations, many more tools, and far more checks around
each one. Building the small version is not a reason to use it for real
work. It is a way to understand what the big one is doing.


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** explain an agent as a model, a harness and tools in a loop,
  and build one in R, **trusted because** you wrote every line that touches
  your files, and a test you did not write decides whether its change is right.
- **Check:** every write and every run is shown to you before it happens; the
  Git pane shows what changed; the test runs in a fresh R session.
- **Reproduce:** `run_r()` runs in a fresh R session, so the agent's checks do
  not depend on what is loaded in yours.
- **Record:** `chat$get_turns()` is the full record of what was sent and
  received; your AI-use log records the tool, model and what you kept.
:::


## Check your understanding

**In an agent built with ellmer, who runs a tool's R function?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The model, on Anthropic's servers",
  answer = "The harness (ellmer), on your computer, after the model asks for it",
  "Nobody: the model predicts what the function would return",
  "RStudio, in a separate window"
))`

**True or false: when an agent's tool reads a file, the file's contents are sent to the model provider.** `r torf(TRUE)`

**`inside_project()` refuses any path under `data/raw/`. Which tool call could still change a raw data file?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "read_file('data/raw/voles_raw.csv')",
  "write_file('data/raw/voles_raw.csv', '...')",
  answer = "run_r() with code that writes to data/raw/",
  "list_files('data/raw')"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Add a `run_tests` tool

Replace general-purpose `run_r()` for checking with a tool that can only run
the project's tests, `function() testthat::test_dir("tests")` run through
`callr::r()`. A narrow tool needs less approval than a general one: you might
let it through without asking, and keep asking for `run_r()`.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A restricted mode

Change `ask_first()` so it asks before every call, reads included. You then
see every file the agent wants to read before it is sent to the provider,
which is the habit Block 4 recommends near confidential data.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Packages that do more

- [btw](https://posit-dev.github.io/btw/) gives ellmer agents ready-made tools
  for R: package documentation, your live session's objects and your project's
  files.
- [mcptools](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcptools/) connects R to the Model
  Context Protocol, so R functions can be tools for other assistants, including
  Claude Code.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Another provider

ellmer has a `chat_*()` function for each provider it supports, and the tools
and loop stay the same. Tool calling can be much less reliable with small local
models, so start with a hosted model.
:::
